clinicalPearls: This is hereditary angioedema occurring despite normal C1 inhibitor level and function, distinguishing it from the classic C1-INH deficiency types.
Attacks are recurrent, non-pitting, non-urticarial swellings of skin and mucosa, and like other hereditary forms they do not respond to antihistamines, corticosteroids or adrenaline.

Several subtypes are recognised, including a factor XII (F12) gene mutation form and others linked to plasminogen (PLG), angiopoietin-1 (ANGPT1), kininogen-1 (KNG1) and additional genes; some families have no identified mutation.
The factor XII form is often oestrogen-sensitive, with attacks precipitated or worsened by pregnancy, the combined oral contraceptive pill or hormone replacement.
A markedly female-predominant expression is characteristic, particularly in the factor XII subtype.
The final common mediator is bradykinin, so treatment mirrors C1-INH-deficient HAE using bradykinin-pathway-directed therapies rather than mast-cell-directed drugs.
Standard complement markers (C4, C1-INH antigen and function) are normal, so diagnosis rests on family history, clinical pattern and genetic testing.
Inheritance is autosomal dominant with incomplete and often sex-influenced penetrance, meaning some carriers remain asymptomatic.
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary angioedema with normal C1 inhibitor is a group of autosomal dominant disorders in which recurrent bradykinin-mediated angioedema occurs despite normal C1-INH concentration and activity. The best-characterised subtype is caused by gain-of-function variants in the F12 gene encoding coagulation factor XII (Hageman factor); these mutations enhance contact-system activation, driving excess kallikrein generation and cleavage of high-molecular-weight kininogen to liberate bradykinin, the vasoactive peptide that increases vascular permeability and produces tissue swelling. Additional subtypes have been linked to variants in plasminogen (PLG), angiopoietin-1 (ANGPT1), kininogen-1 (KNG1), myoferlin, heparan sulfate-glucosamine 3-O-sulfotransferase and others, each converging on dysregulated bradykinin generation or signalling; a further group has no identified genetic cause. The oestrogen sensitivity of the factor XII form reflects hormonal upregulation of contact-system and kininogen activity, explaining the strong female predominance and the triggering role of pregnancy and oestrogen-containing medication. Because the pathway is bradykinin-driven rather than histamine-driven, mast-cell-directed therapies are ineffective.
additionalDifferentials: Hereditary angioedema type I (quantitative C1-INH deficiency)
Hereditary angioedema type II (dysfunctional C1-INH with normal or raised level)
Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency associated with lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease
Histaminergic or idiopathic angioedema with or without urticaria
Systemic capillary leak and other causes of episodic swelling
additionalInvestigations: C4 level, which is characteristically normal between and often during attacks unlike C1-INH deficiency
C1 inhibitor antigenic level and functional activity, both normal in this condition
C1q level to help exclude acquired C1-INH deficiency
Targeted or panel genetic testing for F12, PLG, ANGPT1, KNG1 and related genes
Detailed family pedigree emphasising affected female relatives and hormonal triggers
Review of oestrogen exposure, including contraception, pregnancy and hormone replacement
Assessment for ACE-inhibitor use to exclude drug-induced angioedema
redFlags: Laryngeal or tongue swelling with any voice change, difficulty swallowing or stridor threatening the airway
Rapidly progressive facial or oropharyngeal oedema
Recurrent severe abdominal pain from bowel-wall oedema mimicking a surgical abdomen
Attacks worsening markedly during pregnancy or after starting oestrogen-containing medication
Angioedema unresponsive to adrenaline, antihistamines and corticosteroids
reference.prognosis: With correct diagnosis, avoidance of oestrogen triggers where relevant and access to bradykinin-targeted acute and prophylactic therapy, most patients achieve good control and a normal life expectancy. The chief life-threatening risk remains laryngeal attacks, so an airway-focused action plan is essential.
pitfalls: Excluding hereditary angioedema because C4 and C1-INH are normal; these are expected to be normal in this variant and do not rule it out.
Mistaking attacks for allergic or histaminergic angioedema and relying on antihistamines, steroids and adrenaline, which are ineffective.
Overlooking a strong female-predominant family history and hormonal triggering that point to the factor XII subtype.
Continuing or prescribing oestrogen-containing contraception or an ACE inhibitor, which can precipitate or worsen attacks.
Underestimating airway risk and failing to provide an emergency management plan and on-demand therapy.
